newsitem.title: ALBANIA: European belles to trot down Tirana catwalk.
newsitem.headline: European belles to trot down Tirana catwalk.

text.p: Albania, once ruled by a prudish communist regime that spurned fashion, gambling, TV game shows and rock music as capitalist excesses, plays host on Saturday to the Miss Europe '96 beauty contest.

Some of the 35 contestants, more used to the glittering catwalks of Western cities than a capital emerging from 45 years of grey isolation, may be a little apprehensive of what awaits them. But the mood among Albanians is enthusiastic.

Traffic screeches to a halt when the women emerge from their hotel on the main Skanderbeg Square, accompanied by police motor-cyclists who cut a swathe through the crowds. In former times such hospitality was the reserve of the Party elite.
"It's marvellous. European beauties in Albania. I would never have dreamt of it," said a 63-year-old woman, admiring the contestants.

The pageant will be held in the Palace of Congresses built by the late Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha, who reduced Albania to a nation with few roads, primitive communication and poorly-maintained infrastructure.
Now, emerging from its isolation, Albania is eager to trade on probably its greatest asset -- its countryside and spectacular Adriatic coast. Tourism, however, is in its infancy.

After touring Balkan countryside, most contestants have overcome early reservations about a country that had been a byword in Europe for isolation, shunning all political blocks and closing its frontiers to East and West alike.
The only niggle has been a bout of what some of the women have delicately decribed as "stomach problems" and others, more forthrightly as the "Tirana trots".
"I love the landscape here, the mountains. But we haven't seen very much of it," said Miss Iceland, Solveig Lilja Gudmundsdottir.
She said she had escaped the stomach troubles plaguing some fellow-contestants: "They think it is because of the food."
Malta's beauty queen Donna Evans Xwereb confessed to being among those who had not had a great impression of Albania.
"But when I came here it was totally different. I loved the place. I'm learning a lot of things in Albania, what happened and what didn't happen, how many suffered," Xwereb said.
Chief Albanian organiser Vera Grabocka, who persuaded the French Mondial Events Organisation (MEO) to stage Miss Europe in Albania, said the contest would help better his country's image.
"Enough of refugees, enough of prostitutes, enough, enough...here is another view: ancient Albania, tradition, culture," Grabocka said.
Miss Albania herself, Hygerta Sako, came close to disqualification when museums declined to provide a folk dress for her to wear as required under the contest rules.
The potential embarrassment was averted when organisers themselves scoured the country to find an adequate costume.
